title: Belonging, Part Two
author: Claire Stoneman
summary: Claire Stoneman, a school principal and English teacher, responds to a two-part blog series by David Didau on belonging, agreeing with his argument that belonging depends on children being explicitly inducted into the language of academic success and their subject disciplines, but working through what she felt was still missing from his account. Reading further into Didau's engagement with Charles Taylor and Mikhail Bakhtin -- particularly the idea that meaning and belonging are relational achievements built through dialogue rather than private inner feelings -- helps her locate the piece she wants to add: belonging is buoyed by 'a sea of noticing,' the felt experience of being seen and paid attention to, distinct from but complementary to linguistic induction into a subject. She distinguishes two kinds of noticing: pastoral noticing (checking on lateness, wellbeing, small daily check-ins) and academic noticing (using tools like mini whiteboards to actively see and respond to every child's thinking in real time), arguing the two work together -- pastoral noticing anchors belonging while academic noticing helps it 'set sail.' Stoneman roots the argument in her own school context, where nearly 70% of pupils receive the Pupil Premium, framing rich subject knowledge and being genuinely noticed as twin, inseparable routes to student belonging.
points: Stoneman's key structural contribution is distinguishing pastoral noticing (checking on lateness, wellbeing, small daily check-ins) from academic noticing (using tools like mini whiteboards to see every child's thinking) as two complementary, not competing, routes to belonging.

She builds directly on Didau's synthesis of Charles Taylor and Mikhail Bakhtin -- belonging as a 'relational achievement' built through dialogue rather than a private inner feeling -- but argues something experiential was still missing from that purely linguistic-philosophical account.

Her metaphor is precise and reusable: 'pastoral noticing helps to forge the anchor of belonging; academic noticing helps belonging set sail' -- distinguishing the stabilising function of pastoral care from the propulsive function of academic engagement.

Stoneman explicitly rejects performative belonging gestures ('motivational posters,' generic praise) in favour of specific, individually-directed noticing -- narrating to a class why mini whiteboards are being used, then calling out a specific pupil's specific answer by name.

She grounds the argument in her own school's demographics (nearly 70% Pupil Premium), framing rich curriculum access and being noticed as inseparable, both necessary for genuinely disadvantaged pupils to feel they belong.
quotes: This isn't about motivational posters or empty encouragement, but a genuine human connection through attention.

Meaning is never sealed within an individual mind. It emerges through dialogue, through the back and forth of speaking and being answered. On this view, belonging is not an inner feeling that follows identification. It is a relational achievement.

But this, I think, is the crux of it: belonging is buoyed on a sea of noticing. And this sea of noticing helps belonging to take anchor, float, and set sail. To belong is to feel noticed. To feel seen. To feel valued. To feel respected.

Just as Adam Boxer says, “What does it say about us if we don’t hear their voices? If they can sit in front of us for an hour, and we barely recognise or register their existence? That their thoughts and opinions are excluded from our classroom conversation?

As teachers, we notice all the time. We are experts in noticing: that Jen still can’t quite grasp that thesis statement; that Chris has been late to school twice that week; that Zeynab has cuts on her arm; that Nat is bouncing his knee up and down after that assembly.
Pastoral noticing helps to forge the anchor of belonging; academic noticing helps belonging set sail.
